examples.question_text:
Choose an ungrouped or grouped frequency table for each dataset and explain your choice.
(a) $5,5,6,6,6,7,7,7,7$.
(b) Whole-number measurements: $12,47,31,58,24,39,16,53,28,42,19,35$.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Use an ungrouped table. There are only three distinct values across a small range.
(b) Use a grouped table. There are many different numerical values across a wider range.

examples.question_text:
A table for continuous lengths uses classes $2-11$, $12-21$, and $22-31$ cm.
(a) Explain why these classes leave gaps.
(b) Replace them with classes covering $2<x\le32$ cm, including each upper endpoint.
(c) Explain the problem with using $2\le x\le12$ and $12\le x\le22$ instead.
examples.solution_text:
(a) A length such as $11.5$ cm belongs to no class.
(b) Use $2<x\le12$, $12<x\le22$, and $22<x\le32$. Each boundary belongs to exactly one class.
(c) The classes overlap at $12$ cm, which belongs to both classes.

(a) $\begin{aligned}cc&=\frac{30+39}{2}\\&=34.5\end{aligned}$
(b) $\begin{aligned}cc&=\frac{120+140}{2}\\&=130\end{aligned}$
The second class centre is $130$ cm.

examples.question_text:
Whole-number test marks are $12,18,21,25,29,32,34,37,38,41,45,49$.
(a) Construct a grouped frequency table using $10-19$, $20-29$, $30-39$, and $40-49$.
(b) Find the total number of students, the most frequent class, and the number scoring $30$ or more.
(c) Can the grouped table alone tell you exactly how many scored less than $35$? Explain.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Count each mark in its class.

| Mark | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $10-19$ | $2$ |
| $20-29$ | $3$ |
| $30-39$ | $4$ |
| $40-49$ | $3$ |

(b) $n=2+3+4+3=12$.
The most frequent class is $30-39$.
The number scoring $30$ or more is $4+3=7$.
(c) No. The grouped table does not show how the four marks in $30-39$ are split between $30-34$ and $35-39$. Individual values are lost.

examples.question_text:
Plant heights, in centimetres, are $4.8,10.0,10.2,15.6,20.0,20.4,24.7,30.0,30.5,38.2$.
(a) Construct a frequency table using $0<h\le10$, $10<h\le20$, $20<h\le30$, and $30<h\le40$.
(b) Find the fraction and decimal relative frequency of plants taller than $20$ cm.
(c) Find the percentage of plants $10$ cm or less tall.
examples.solution_text:
(a) An upper endpoint belongs to the class ending at that value: $10.0$ belongs to the first class, $20.0$ to the second, and $30.0$ to the third.

| Height (cm) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0<h\le10$ | $2$ |
| $10<h\le20$ | $3$ |
| $20<h\le30$ | $3$ |
| $30<h\le40$ | $2$ |

(b) $n=2+3+3+2=10$.
There are $3+2=5$ plants taller than $20$ cm.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Fraction}&=\frac{5}{10}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}\text{Relative frequency}&=\frac{5}{10}\\&=0.5\end{aligned}$
(c) $\begin{aligned}\text{Percentage}&=\frac{2}{10}\times100\%\\&=20\%\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
The grouped table records waiting times.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0<t\le5$ | $6$ |
| $5<t\le10$ | $9$ |
| $10<t\le15$ | $12$ |
| $15<t\le20$ | $3$ |

(a) Complete the cumulative-frequency column.
(b) Find the frequency of $10<t\le15$ by subtracting cumulative frequencies.
(c) Find the relative frequency of each class as a decimal.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Add each frequency to the previous running total.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0<t\le5$ | $6$ | $6$ |
| $5<t\le10$ | $9$ | $15$ |
| $10<t\le15$ | $12$ | $27$ |
| $15<t\le20$ | $3$ | $30$ |

(b) The frequency is $27-15=12$.
(c) Divide each frequency by the total $30$.

| Waiting time (minutes) | Relative frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $0<t\le5$ | $6/30=0.2$ |
| $5<t\le10$ | $9/30=0.3$ |
| $10<t\le15$ | $12/30=0.4$ |
| $15<t\le20$ | $3/30=0.1$ |

examples.question_text:
For $90$ measurements, all values satisfy $0<x\le50$. The first class $0<x\le10$ has frequency $12$. There are $34$ measurements with $x\le20$, $25$ with $x>30$, and $7$ with $x>40$.
Complete the frequency and cumulative-frequency columns for five classes of width $10$.
examples.solution_text:
Subtract cumulative counts to find individual class frequencies. Subtract the count above $30$ from the total to find the count through $30$.
$\begin{aligned}f_1&=12\\f_2&=34-12=22\\\text{Count with }x\le30&=90-25=65\\f_3&=65-34=31\\f_4&=25-7=18\\f_5&=7\end{aligned}$

| Class | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0<x\le10$ | $12$ | $12$ |
| $10<x\le20$ | $22$ | $34$ |
| $20<x\le30$ | $31$ | $65$ |
| $30<x\le40$ | $18$ | $83$ |
| $40<x\le50$ | $7$ | $90$ |

coverage.summary: Authored seven examples covering all distinct accepted assessment methods with changed values and separate editable prompts and solutions. Tables supply the necessary representations; no diagram or solution annotation is needed. Relation-led working uses aligned gutters; independent equations receive no phantom equals. Plain solution prose and mathematics inherit the supplied renderer's blue styling. Practice and quiz content was classified only, without alteration or renewed mathematical audit. Independent review and actual rendering verification remain for the coordinator.

examples.derivation: Dataset (a) has three distinct values, 5–7, so an ungrouped table is suitable. Dataset (b) has twelve distinct values spanning 12–58, supporting grouping. This follows source Foundation Q1.

11.5 lies between the original classes. The replacement intervals partition 2<x≤32 without gaps or overlap and include each upper endpoint. Both proposed inclusive intervals contain 12, demonstrating overlap.
The endpoint averages are (30+39)/2=34.5 and (120+140)/2=130 cm. Both aligned calculations retain the left-hand side on their opening equation; no phantom equals is required.

Independent counts give frequencies 2,3,4,3, totalling 12. The modal class is 30–39; 4+3=7 students scored at least 30. The grouped table cannot distinguish the four individual marks within 30–39, so it cannot determine the exact count below 35.

Endpoint-inclusive counting gives 2,3,3,2, totalling 10. Five heights exceed 20 cm, giving 5/10=1/2=0.5. Two heights are at most 10 cm, giving 20%. Decimal relative frequency uses the explicitly retained accepted assessment method.

Running totals are 6,15,27,30. Subtracting adjacent cumulative counts gives 27−15=12 for the third class. Dividing frequencies by 30 gives 0.2,0.3,0.4,0.1, which sum to 1. Tables adequately represent all requested results.

The second frequency is 34−12=22. The count through 30 is 90−25=65, so the third frequency is 65−34=31. The fourth is 25−7=18 and the fifth is 7. Frequencies total 90; cumulative counts are 12,34,65,83,90. The aligned rows are independent equations and require no phantom equals.

review.summary: All nine distinct assessed methods are covered by the seven examples, and all 29 exact assessment locators are mapped. Source adaptations use different values and remain within the accepted methods. Decimal relative frequency is supported by the supplied explicit acceptance context. There were no existing examples to audit. Separate editable prompts and solutions, inline mathematics, gutters and table representations are suitable; solution prose and mathematics inherit the confirmed blue styling. Accepted practice and quiz mathematics were not re-audited. Actual rendering and final-size typography verification remain with the coordinator.
